passage:
The West African griot tradition has long been interpreted by outside observers as a form of oral historiography — a living archive in which hereditary praise-singers preserve communal genealogies and dynastic chronicles for the noble families they serve. This characterization, while not false, captures only the surface of a practice whose layered functions challenge any simple taxonomy. The griot is simultaneously historian, diplomat, musician, and moral arbiter, and the tension between these roles is precisely what gives the tradition its cultural authority.

What outside accounts have most persistently misread is the griot's relationship to factual accuracy. Western historiographic norms treat deviations from the documentary record as errors or propaganda; by these standards, the griot who embellishes a patron's lineage appears merely as a flatterer. But within the tradition's own epistemology, the griot's embellishments are not distortions of history so much as performances of social possibility — articulations of what a lineage has the right to aspire to, and therefore what its members are obligated to become. Truth, in this framework, is prospective as much as retrospective. A praise-song does not simply report that a ruler descended from heroes; it enlists the present ruler in a heroic project, binding him to obligations the ancestors allegedly embodied.

This performative dimension also explains the griot's political leverage, which observers have often found puzzling. A skilled griot can, in the same performance, praise a chief into generosity and shame him for past failures — a kind of rhetorical judo that keeps power accountable without triggering open confrontation. The griot's social immunity, the custom by which griots are exempt from the violence that might meet an ordinary subject's criticism, is therefore not a mere courtesy but a structural necessity: without that immunity, the mechanism of public accountability would collapse. Critics who describe griots as sycophants have confused the surface register of praise with its deeper structural function.

More recent scholarship, particularly among researchers trained in both linguistic anthropology and African history, has begun to honor this complexity. Rather than measuring griot narratives against external archives, these scholars treat the performances themselves as primary texts — documents of social aspiration, political negotiation, and ethical instruction. The shift has yielded richer interpretations, though it has also raised a secondary question: whether the analytic tools developed for written literary traditions are adequate to the analysis of a form that exists, fundamentally, in performance, in breath, in the irretrievable moment of its own delivery.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The griot tradition is best understood as a sophisticated form of oral historiography that Western scholars have only recently begun to appreciate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Western historiographic standards are fundamentally inadequate for evaluating any non-literate cultural practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The griot tradition serves multiple, interrelated functions — historical, political, and ethical — whose complexity has been obscured by interpretations focused solely on factual accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Griots exercise political power by combining praise with criticism, a strategy that has long protected them from retaliation by patrons.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recent scholarship on the griot tradition has raised important methodological questions about whether literary tools can be applied to oral performance.

explanations.correct: The passage's thesis, distributed across all four paragraphs, is that the griot tradition has multiple layered functions — historical, performative/political, and ethical — that outside accounts miss by focusing only on factual accuracy. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow: paragraph 1 already concedes that the 'oral historiography' label is 'not false' but insufficient; the passage argues for a fuller picture, not merely a richer historiographic one.
explanations.B: Overstates: the passage critiques Western standards as applied to griots, not as universally inadequate for all non-literate practices. This exceeds what the author argues.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement: this accurately summarizes paragraph 3's point about political leverage but ignores the historical and ethical dimensions central to the passage.
explanations.E: Restates a closing suggestion as the main point: the methodological question appears only in the final sentence as a secondary concern, not as the passage's primary argument.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Western observers who describe griots as sycophants can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: sympathetic, because their assessments are based on reasonable historiographic principles

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissive, because such observers have no genuine interest in understanding African cultural practices

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical but measured, because their error stems from applying inappropriate standards rather than from outright bias

choices.label: D
choices.text: openly contemptuous, because they have willfully misrepresented the griot's social function

choices.label: E
choices.text: ambivalent, because the sycophancy charge contains some validity even if it misses the deeper point

explanations.correct: The author explicitly identifies a diagnostic error — confusing 'surface register of praise with its deeper structural function' — and locates the source in misapplied Western standards. This is a measured critique of methodology, not of motives. C captures both the critical stance and its restrained tone.
explanations.A: Wrong valence: the author disagrees with this view; calling the standards 'reasonable' would endorse them.
explanations.B: Overstated and unsupported: the author attributes the error to category mistakes, not to lack of interest. The passage does not impute motives.
explanations.D: 'Openly contemptuous' and 'willfully' overstate the author's intensity and imply deliberate distortion, which the passage does not claim.
explanations.E: The passage does not concede any validity to the sycophancy charge; it treats the charge as simply miscategorized, making 'ambivalent' inaccurate.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the griot's social immunity from violence serves which of the following purposes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It elevates the griot's status above that of other court figures, ensuring that patrons take praise-songs seriously.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It makes possible the mechanism by which griots hold power publicly accountable without provoking open confrontation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It protects griots who choose to record unflattering historical facts in their performances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a courtesy extended in recognition of the griot's musical and artistic contributions to the community.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It allows griots to negotiate on behalf of noble families in diplomatic disputes.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that without the griot's social immunity 'the mechanism of public accountability would collapse,' directly linking the immunity to the griot's role in keeping power accountable. B paraphrases this accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not state that immunity elevates the griot's status above other court figures; this is an unsupported inference.
explanations.C: The passage frames immunity in relation to political criticism, not to historical record-keeping, making this too narrow and misdirected.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly states that social immunity is 'not a mere courtesy' — this choice reproduces the view the author rejects.
explanations.E: Diplomatic functions are mentioned in paragraph 1 as one of the griot's roles but are not connected to the immunity custom discussed in paragraph 3.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that within the griot tradition's own epistemology, a praise-song that embellishes a ruler's lineage is best understood as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a diplomatic fiction that both speaker and audience understand to be inaccurate

choices.label: B
choices.text: an ethical prescription that binds the present ruler to heroic obligations

choices.label: C
choices.text: a historical document that must be evaluated against external archival evidence

choices.label: D
choices.text: a musical performance whose primary value lies in its aesthetic qualities

choices.label: E
choices.text: a form of propaganda designed to insulate the patron from political criticism

explanations.correct: The passage states that a praise-song 'enlists the present ruler in a heroic project, binding him to obligations the ancestors allegedly embodied.' This is an ethical prescription, and B captures that inference precisely.
explanations.A: The passage does not describe embellishments as fictions understood by all parties to be false; rather, they operate as prospective truths, making 'diplomatic fiction' a mischaracterization.
explanations.C: This describes the Western historiographic standard the author critiques — the opposite of what the tradition's own epistemology holds.
explanations.D: Musical function is mentioned among the griot's multiple roles in paragraph 1 but is not how the tradition's epistemology frames the embellishment of lineage.
explanations.E: The passage distinguishes the griot's function from propaganda; the praise-song holds rulers accountable rather than insulating them.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely describes the griot's ability to 'praise a chief into generosity and shame him for past failures' (third paragraph) primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the specific rhetorical techniques griots use during formal court ceremonies

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that griots exploit their social immunity for personal financial gain

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide evidence that the griot functions as a mechanism of political accountability, not merely as a flatterer

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the griot's political role with the diplomatic functions described in the first paragraph

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that the griot's power over patrons ultimately undermines political stability

explanations.correct: The specific example of praising and shaming in a single performance is introduced to support the immediately preceding claim that the griot exercises 'political leverage' and keeps 'power accountable.' C identifies this rhetorical function accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not describe formal court ceremonies; the example is offered as conceptual evidence of a structural function, not as an ethnographic detail about technique.
explanations.B: The passage nowhere suggests griots use immunity for personal financial gain; this imports an assumption the text does not support.
explanations.D: The diplomatic role in paragraph 1 is not revisited here; the passage is not drawing a contrast at this point but making a cumulative argument.
explanations.E: The passage implies that griot accountability enhances rather than undermines stability; this choice inverts the passage's reasoning.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional view is introduced and then systematically refuted through a series of counterexamples drawn from ethnographic fieldwork.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A partial characterization of a cultural practice is introduced, its inadequacy explained across two dimensions, and a more adequate scholarly approach is described along with its remaining limitation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing scholarly interpretations of a cultural practice are compared, their respective merits assessed, and a synthesis is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cultural practice is described, its historical origins are traced, and its contemporary decline is documented.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A scholarly controversy is introduced, the major positions are summarized, and the author endorses one position while acknowledging the validity of the other.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the partial 'oral historiography' characterization. Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain its inadequacy (misreading of factual accuracy; misreading of political function). Paragraph 4 describes recent scholarship that honors complexity and notes its remaining methodological limitation. B captures all four moves in correct sequence.
explanations.A: The passage does not refute through ethnographic counterexamples; its argument is interpretive and conceptual, not data-driven.
explanations.C: The passage does not pit two scholarly interpretations against each other as equals; it corrects one dominant misreading with a more adequate framework.
explanations.D: No historical origins are traced and no contemporary decline is documented; these moves do not occur in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage does not present two positions as equally valid and then endorse one; the 'oral historiography' reading is presented as simply insufficient, not as a rival with genuine merit.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that recent scholars who treat griot performances as 'primary texts' differ from earlier outside observers primarily in that recent scholars

choices.label: A
choices.text: have access to audio recordings that allow more precise analysis of griot performances than was previously possible

choices.label: B
choices.text: evaluate griot narratives according to the social and ethical purposes the performances serve rather than by their correspondence to external documentary records

choices.label: C
choices.text: focus exclusively on the musical dimensions of griot performance, setting aside political and historical content

choices.label: D
choices.text: accept griot genealogical accounts as literally accurate descriptions of historical events

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that griot traditions are superior to written historiography as a means of preserving cultural memory

explanations.correct: The passage states that recent scholars 'treat the performances themselves as primary texts — documents of social aspiration, political negotiation, and ethical instruction' rather than measuring them against external archives. B accurately infers the methodological distinction.
explanations.A: Audio recordings are never mentioned; this introduces technology the passage does not discuss.
explanations.C: The passage says recent scholars treat performances as documents of social aspiration and political negotiation, not that they focus exclusively on music.
explanations.D: The passage does not suggest recent scholars take genealogical accounts as literally accurate; rather, they treat performances as social and ethical documents.
explanations.E: The passage does not claim griot traditions are superior to written historiography; it argues only that they require different analytical tools.

passage:
Among the interpretive schools that shaped twentieth-century literary criticism, New Criticism occupied a peculiar position: simultaneously the most pedagogically influential and the most philosophically embattled. Its central doctrine — that a poem should be read as a self-sufficient verbal artifact, with the reader's attention confined to the text itself and shielded from authorial biography, historical context, and readerly affect — gave undergraduate classrooms a clean, teachable method. Yet the very clarity that made New Criticism so exportable also made it a target, and by the 1960s it had become the shared antagonist around which several rival schools defined themselves.

The charge most persistently leveled against New Criticism was that its supposedly neutral 'close reading' was in fact an ideologically loaded procedure. Its insistence on organic unity — the idea that a successful poem reconciles all its tensions into a coherent whole — was said to privilege certain kinds of poetry (metaphysical, ironic, richly ambiguous) over others (political, confessional, formally simple). Critics in the reader-response tradition argued that meaning is not a property of the text but an event produced in the encounter between text and reader; meaning, on this account, is always already shaped by the reader's history, gender, and cultural position. Deconstructionists went further, arguing that New Criticism's organic unity was a suppression of the textual undecidability it was most fond of celebrating: the very ambiguity that New Critics held in tension was, for Derrida and his followers, evidence that no stable meaning could ever be fully achieved.

What is often overlooked in rehearsals of these debates, however, is the degree to which New Criticism's original practitioners were themselves ambivalent about the doctrine's limits. Cleanth Brooks, whose The Well Wrought Urn (1947) remains the movement's most exemplary text, repeatedly acknowledged that his readings were interpretations, not revelations; his 'heresy of paraphrase' — the argument that a poem's meaning cannot be reduced to a prose restatement — was itself a kind of epistemic modesty, a concession that the poem exceeds any single reading of it. Similarly, W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley's notorious 'intentional fallacy' essay was not an argument for ignoring authorial intention as philosophically irrelevant; it was a practical recommendation about where to look first, a methodological constraint rather than a metaphysical decree.

The irony is that the later theoretical schools that positioned themselves against New Criticism often reproduced its most valuable insight — that language is irreducibly complex — while discarding the practical discipline of attending closely to individual texts. A critic who invokes Derrida to demonstrate that all texts destabilize meaning has said something both true and uninformative unless she can show, line by line, how a particular poem enacts that instability. In this sense, the pedagogical legacy of New Criticism is not its doctrine but its discipline: the slow, patient, word-by-word engagement with the text that remains, whatever one's theoretical commitments, the indispensable ground of literary knowledge.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is most likely to

choices.label: A
choices.text: defend New Criticism against its critics by demonstrating that their objections rest on misreadings of its central tenets

choices.label: B
choices.text: trace the historical decline of New Criticism as a dominant school of literary interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that while subsequent theoretical schools exposed real limitations in New Criticism, its core practice of close reading retains enduring value

choices.label: D
choices.text: compare the ideological assumptions underlying New Criticism and reader-response theory

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why New Criticism became the dominant method of literary instruction in undergraduate classrooms during the twentieth century

explanations.correct: The passage acknowledges New Criticism's real vulnerabilities (paragraphs 2 and 3) but ultimately argues in paragraph 4 that its 'pedagogical legacy' — the discipline of close reading — 'remains the indispensable ground of literary knowledge.' C integrates both the concessive and the affirmative strands of the argument.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage concedes that several critiques had genuine force, rather than dismissing them as misreadings.
explanations.B: The passage tracks the critical reception of New Criticism but does not frame the passage as a historical narrative of decline; the final paragraph rehabilitates the practice.
explanations.D: Too narrow: reader-response theory is one of three critical schools discussed and is not compared exhaustively with New Criticism.
explanations.E: Pedagogical exportability is introduced in paragraph 1 as context, not as the passage's primary explanatory goal.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 'heresy of paraphrase' as formulated by Cleanth Brooks is best understood as

choices.label: A
choices.text: an argument that paraphrase is an illegitimate critical tool because it introduces the reader's subjective response into the analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: a concession that a poem's full meaning exceeds any single interpretive account of it

choices.label: C
choices.text: a rejection of the deconstructionist claim that textual meaning is inherently unstable

choices.label: D
choices.text: a claim that the meaning of a poem is identical to the author's intended meaning

choices.label: E
choices.text: a doctrine holding that successful poems resist any reduction to simple, paraphrasable content because they are organically unified

explanations.correct: The passage states that the 'heresy of paraphrase' was 'a kind of epistemic modesty, a concession that the poem exceeds any single reading of it.' B paraphrases this accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not connect the heresy of paraphrase to the reader's subjective response; that concern belongs to reader-response theory.
explanations.C: The heresy of paraphrase was formulated by Brooks, an original New Critic, well before deconstruction emerged; the passage does not link it to rejecting deconstructionist claims.
explanations.D: Authorial intention is specifically excluded from New Criticism's framework via the 'intentional fallacy'; connecting the heresy of paraphrase to authorial intent inverts the movement's doctrine.
explanations.E: While organic unity is a New Critical concept, the passage specifically defines the heresy of paraphrase as epistemic modesty about what any reading achieves, not as a claim about organic unity.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about deconstruction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deconstruction's claim that texts destabilize meaning is false, because New Criticism demonstrated that organic unity can always be achieved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deconstruction advanced a valid insight about the complexity of language but became less useful when it abandoned the practice of attending closely to particular texts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deconstruction was the most philosophically rigorous of the schools that challenged New Criticism and therefore represents the most significant advance in literary theory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deconstruction's critique of New Criticism was undermined by its own reliance on the close-reading methods it purported to reject.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deconstruction correctly identified the 'organic unity' doctrine as ideologically motivated and thereby exposed the political limitations of New Criticism.

explanations.correct: The passage states that later theoretical schools, including deconstruction, 'often reproduced [New Criticism's] most valuable insight — that language is irreducibly complex — while discarding the practical discipline of attending closely to individual texts.' B captures both the valid insight and the critical deficiency the author attributes to deconstruction.
explanations.A: The author does not claim deconstruction's core insight is false; the passage treats it as 'both true and uninformative' when applied without textual specificity.
explanations.C: The passage does not rank deconstruction above other critical schools; it treats all rivals to New Criticism similarly in paragraph 4.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim deconstructionists relied on close-reading methods; the critique is that they abandoned such methods.
explanations.E: The 'ideologically motivated' critique of New Criticism is attributed to critics generally in paragraph 2, not specifically or exclusively to deconstruction.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy' essay (third paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide an example of the ideological bias that subsequent critics identified in New Criticism's core doctrines

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate how New Criticism's practical recommendations were sometimes misread as stronger metaphysical claims than their authors intended

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that New Criticism ultimately failed to produce a coherent theoretical framework

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast New Criticism's treatment of intention with reader-response theory's emphasis on the reader's role in producing meaning

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that New Criticism's influence on undergraduate pedagogy was primarily the result of its philosophical rigor

explanations.correct: The passage describes the 'intentional fallacy' essay as 'a practical recommendation about where to look first, a methodological constraint rather than a metaphysical decree' — thereby illustrating how a practical methodological guideline was taken for a stronger philosophical claim. B captures this function precisely.
explanations.A: The passage presents the intentional fallacy essay as a misread practical recommendation, not as evidence of ideological bias; that charge is raised in paragraph 2, not paragraph 3.
explanations.C: The passage does not argue that New Criticism failed to produce coherence; the paragraph rehabilitates New Criticism's original practitioners.
explanations.D: Reader-response theory is not invoked in paragraph 3; the contrast being drawn is between the essay's practical intent and its subsequent metaphysical reception.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly separates New Criticism's pedagogical appeal (paragraph 1) from its philosophical credentials; this answer conflates the two.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward New Criticism can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement of its doctrines as the most reliable basis for literary analysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: respectful appreciation of its practical discipline, combined with acknowledgment that its theoretical claims were legitimately challenged

choices.label: C
choices.text: nostalgic regret that ideological critics dismantled a movement whose insights were too subtle for its opponents to grasp

choices.label: D
choices.text: measured skepticism toward both New Criticism and its rivals, suggesting that no critical school has produced genuinely useful tools

choices.label: E
choices.text: ambivalence rooted in the belief that New Criticism's pedagogy was valuable but its aesthetic preferences were indefensible

explanations.correct: The passage criticizes New Criticism's theoretical vulnerabilities across paragraphs 2 and 3 while affirming in paragraph 4 that the discipline of close reading 'remains the indispensable ground of literary knowledge.' B captures both the respectful appreciation and the honest acknowledgment of legitimate critique.
explanations.A: The author concedes real weaknesses in New Criticism's doctrines; 'uncritical endorsement' overstates the author's commitment.
explanations.C: 'Nostalgic regret' and the implication that critics simply failed to grasp New Criticism's subtlety overstate both the emotional register and the dismissal of rivals; the author concedes some rival critiques had force.
explanations.D: The author does affirm that close reading produces useful insight; 'no critical school has produced genuinely useful tools' is more skeptical than the passage supports.
explanations.E: While aesthetic preferences (organic unity privileging certain poetry) are mentioned as a legitimate critique in paragraph 2, the author does not conclude that New Criticism's aesthetic preferences were 'indefensible' — that is the critics' view, not the author's final assessment.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's claim in the final paragraph that a theoretically sophisticated critic still requires the discipline of close reading?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several prominent deconstructionist critics produced exhaustive close readings of individual texts that were widely admired for their precision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Undergraduate students who were taught New Critical methods have performed better on standardized tests of reading comprehension than students taught other methods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A study of critical essays found that theoretical claims unsupported by textual analysis were consistently rated less persuasive and less illuminating by professional literary scholars.

choices.label: D
choices.text: New Criticism's doctrine of organic unity has been shown to be inapplicable to the analysis of postmodern fiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many literary theorists who invoke Derrida are familiar with only a small fraction of his published writings.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that theoretical sophistication becomes 'uninformative' without 'slow, patient, word-by-word engagement with the text.' A finding that theory unsupported by textual analysis is less persuasive and illuminating to professional scholars directly supports this claim.
explanations.A: This would somewhat support the claim, but it describes deconstructionists who did practice close reading — it shows they could combine theory and close reading, which is consistent but does not directly demonstrate that textual analysis is necessary for theoretical claims to be useful.
explanations.B: Undergraduate test performance addresses pedagogical effectiveness in a general reading context, not the specific claim about theoretical criticism's need for textual grounding.
explanations.D: This would support a critique of New Criticism's organic unity doctrine, not the final paragraph's claim about close reading's necessity — it weakens a New Critical doctrine rather than supporting the author's closing argument.
explanations.E: Scholars' familiarity with Derrida's corpus is irrelevant to whether textual analysis is necessary for critical claims to be illuminating.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critical movement is introduced and praised, its achievements are catalogued, and a prediction about its future influence is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A critical movement is introduced with its central doctrine, the charges leveled against it are presented, evidence that its original practitioners were more self-aware than critics acknowledged is offered, and its lasting contribution is identified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two rival critical schools are introduced, their doctrines compared across several criteria, and a synthesis combining their insights is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A widely-held view of a critical movement is introduced and then comprehensively refuted by appeals to historical evidence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critical movement's historical origins are traced, its decline is explained, and the emergence of reader-response theory as its successor is documented.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces New Criticism and its central doctrine of the text as self-sufficient artifact. Paragraph 2 presents the charges (ideological bias, reader-response, deconstruction). Paragraph 3 shows that original practitioners like Brooks and Wimsatt/Beardsley were already ambivalent about the doctrine's limits. Paragraph 4 identifies the lasting contribution as close-reading discipline. B tracks all four moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not catalogue achievements in a straightforward way and offers no prediction; the structure is more adversarial (introducing charges and responding to them).
explanations.C: The passage does not compare two rival schools comprehensively; reader-response and deconstruction are introduced as critics of New Criticism, not as co-equal subjects.
explanations.D: The passage does not comprehensively refute a view; it complicates the critics' portrayal of New Criticism and recovers a residual value from it.
explanations.E: No historical origins are traced, no decline is 'explained' as the focus, and reader-response theory is not documented as a successor — it is one of several critics of New Criticism.

passage:
The emergence of minimalism in American concert music during the 1960s and 1970s is generally narrated as a clean break: after decades of serialism's total organization of pitch, duration, and dynamics, composers such as Terry Riley, Philip Glass, and Steve Reich stripped music to its barest constitutive elements — steady pulse, diatonic harmony, gradual change — and in doing so reconnected it with the listening public that serialism had alienated. This account has the appeal of a good story, but it simplifies the relationship between minimalism and its predecessors in ways that obscure what was most original about the movement.

Serialism's hold on academic composition in the postwar years was real, but it was neither as monolithic nor as audience-hostile as the standard narrative suggests. Composers such as Olivier Messiaen and Alban Berg found within serial procedures a lyrical expressivity that their purely theoretical successors often abandoned; and the concert-going public's alienation from new music had roots that preceded serial composition by decades, in the general fragmentation of audience culture that accompanied urbanization and the rise of recorded sound. Minimalism did not so much rescue music from serialism as redefine what musical sophistication could mean — trading the vertical complexity of tone clusters and dense counterpoint for a horizontal complexity in which the listener's perception itself becomes the compositional variable.

This shift in the locus of compositional interest — from the score to the listener's perceptual experience — is the genuinely radical element of minimalist aesthetics, and it connects the movement to contemporaneous developments in the visual arts and philosophy of mind. Steve Reich's early tape pieces, in which two recordings of the same source material drift gradually out of phase with each other, require the listener not to decode a structure but to experience the emergence of pattern from near-identity. The music is not about a process; it is a process, one that unfolds differently for each listener depending on where attention is directed. This is not the impersonality that standard accounts attribute to minimalism; it is, rather, a deliberate transfer of compositional agency to the perceptual act.

The irony is that minimalism's most ardent champions have sometimes reproduced the oversimplification they set out to correct. In celebrating the movement's accessibility and its rejection of academic insularity, they have tended to undervalue the rigor of its engagement with perception, temporality, and pattern recognition — topics that belong as fully to the philosophy of mind as to music theory. A richer account of minimalism would situate it not merely as a populist corrective to serialism but as a serious contribution to a set of questions about how consciousness constructs musical experience that remain, decades later, unresolved.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minimalism succeeded where serialism failed because it reconnected concert music with a listening public that had been alienated by postwar academic composition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard narrative of minimalism as a populist reaction against serialism oversimplifies the movement, whose genuinely original contribution lies in its redirection of compositional interest toward the listener's perceptual experience.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Steve Reich's tape pieces represent the purest expression of minimalist aesthetics and deserve greater recognition in histories of twentieth-century music.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serialism was neither as theoretically rigid nor as hostile to audiences as is commonly assumed, and minimalism's reputation as its corrective is therefore undeserved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Minimalism's connections to developments in the visual arts and philosophy of mind make it more important than music historians have recognized.

explanations.correct: The passage's central argument, built across all four paragraphs, is that the standard 'clean break from serialism' narrative is a simplification, and that minimalism's real originality is its transfer of compositional focus to the listener's perceptual experience. B integrates the corrective and the affirmative strands.
explanations.A: This is precisely the 'standard account' the passage critiques; it cannot be the main point of an argument that calls this account a simplification.
explanations.C: Too narrow: Reich's tape pieces are introduced as an illustration of the perceptual argument in paragraph 3, not as the passage's central claim.
explanations.D: Overstates one component of the argument: the passage qualifies the standard narrative about serialism but does not conclude that minimalism's reputation is 'undeserved' — only that its reputation is misdescribed.
explanations.E: The connections to visual arts and philosophy of mind appear in paragraph 3 as support for the perceptual argument, not as the passage's primary point.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the audience alienation from new music that the standard narrative attributes to serialism actually had roots in

choices.label: A
choices.text: the increasing theoretical complexity of serial procedures, which made new music inaccessible to listeners without formal training

choices.label: B
choices.text: the fragmentation of audience culture that preceded serial composition, brought about by urbanization and the rise of recorded sound

choices.label: C
choices.text: the failure of postwar composers to produce works as lyrically expressive as those of earlier serial composers such as Alban Berg

choices.label: D
choices.text: the deliberate rejection by serial composers of the listening public as a relevant constituency for their work

choices.label: E
choices.text: the displacement of live concert performance by radio broadcasting and the commercial recording industry

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that 'the concert-going public's alienation from new music had roots that preceded serial composition by decades, in the general fragmentation of audience culture that accompanied urbanization and the rise of recorded sound.' B paraphrases this accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim theoretical complexity per se caused audience alienation; it locates the causes in broader cultural fragmentation predating serialism.
explanations.C: The lyrical expressivity of Berg and Messiaen is mentioned to complicate the monolithic view of serialism, not as a cause of audience alienation.
explanations.D: The passage does not state that serial composers deliberately rejected the listening public; this imputes an intention the passage does not assert.
explanations.E: Radio broadcasting is not mentioned; 'recorded sound' appears in the passage but as part of a broader cultural fragmentation, not as a separate cause in its own right as stated here.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about Steve Reich's tape pieces?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They illustrate that minimalism, despite its apparent simplicity, engages sophisticated questions about perception and consciousness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They demonstrate that minimalist composers were more directly influenced by visual art than by earlier musical traditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are best understood as a reaction against the impersonality of serial composition rather than as an independent aesthetic development.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They were less accessible to general audiences than the minimalist works of Philip Glass and Terry Riley.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They represent the fullest realization of the aesthetic principles that all minimalist composers sought to achieve.

explanations.correct: The passage uses Reich's tape pieces to demonstrate that minimalism involves 'a deliberate transfer of compositional agency to the perceptual act' and connects this to 'the philosophy of mind.' A correctly infers that the author views the tape pieces as evidence of minimalism's sophisticated engagement with perceptual and philosophical questions.
explanations.B: Visual arts are mentioned as a contemporaneous development, not as a more direct influence than musical tradition; the passage does not claim visual art was the primary influence on Reich.
explanations.C: The passage explicitly rejects the framing of minimalism primarily as a reaction against serialism; it argues for an independent aesthetic contribution centered on perceptual experience.
explanations.D: Comparative accessibility between different minimalist composers is never addressed in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage singles out Reich's tape pieces as an illustration of the perceptual argument but does not claim all minimalists shared the same aesthetic goals or that Reich fully realized them.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Olivier Messiaen and Alban Berg (second paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the variety of expressive approaches available within serial composition, thereby complicating the standard narrative's portrayal of serialism as uniformly arid

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide examples of composers whose careers bridged the gap between serialism and minimalism

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that serial composition achieved greater popular success than is commonly acknowledged

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the lyrical expressivity of early serial composers with the deliberate impersonality of later minimalists

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that minimalism's rejection of serialism was motivated by aesthetic rather than political considerations

explanations.correct: Messiaen and Berg are cited immediately after the claim that serialism 'was neither as monolithic nor as audience-hostile as the standard narrative suggests.' Their lyrical expressivity is the evidence offered to complicate the monolithic view. A captures this function accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not describe Messiaen or Berg as bridging serialism and minimalism; they are invoked to complicate the portrayal of serialism, not to trace a transition.
explanations.C: Popular success is not the claim being made here; the passage says their work was lyrically expressive, not that it reached a large audience.
explanations.D: The passage does not use Messiaen and Berg to contrast with minimalism's impersonality; in fact, the passage later argues that minimalism's supposed impersonality is itself a mischaracterization.
explanations.E: The passage does not discuss the motivations behind minimalism's rejection of serialism as aesthetic versus political; this topic is not raised.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward minimalism's 'ardent champions' (final paragraph) can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement that their celebration of minimalism's accessibility is the most important critical contribution to the movement's legacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: mild criticism for perpetuating a simplification that undervalues the movement's philosophical and perceptual rigor

choices.label: C
choices.text: contempt for their failure to understand the connection between minimalism and the visual arts

choices.label: D
choices.text: sympathy for their effort to defend minimalism against detractors, even though their arguments occasionally go too far

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutrality, since the author regards their simplification as no worse than the standard narrative's simplification

explanations.correct: The passage states that ardent champions 'have tended to undervalue the rigor of its engagement with perception, temporality, and pattern recognition,' calling this an 'oversimplification.' The tone is critical but measured — 'mild criticism' rather than contempt or hostility. B captures both the valence and the intensity accurately.
explanations.A: The author explicitly criticizes the champions' celebration as an oversimplification; 'enthusiastic agreement' inverts the author's stance.
explanations.C: 'Contempt' overstates the author's intensity, and the criticism is about undervaluing perceptual rigor, not specifically about failing to understand connections to visual arts.
explanations.D: The passage does not frame the champions as defending minimalism against detractors; it criticizes them for oversimplifying in their celebration, not for defending the movement too vigorously.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral; the final paragraph explicitly identifies what a 'richer account' would do differently from the champions' approach.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author describes when discussing how minimalist music transfers compositional agency to the listener's perceptual act?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A choreographer designs a dance in which the exact sequence of movements is fixed by the score, but audience members are invited to choose which dancer to watch, making each viewing experience distinct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A novelist structures a plot so that all major themes are stated explicitly in the first chapter, allowing readers to track their development with ease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A film director uses steadily increasing tempo throughout a scene to create a sense of urgency that every viewer will experience in the same way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A painter arranges patches of nearly identical color across a large canvas so that the patterns perceived within the field shift as the viewer's eye moves.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A poet compresses complex philosophical content into a highly structured sonnet form, demanding intensive interpretive effort from readers trained in literary analysis.

explanations.correct: The passage describes Reich's tape pieces as working through 'near-identity,' where patterns 'emerge' differently 'for each listener depending on where attention is directed.' The mechanism is: nearly identical material, gradual drift, and perception-dependent pattern emergence. D's painter using nearly identical color patches whose perceived patterns shift with the viewer's eye direction instantiates this mechanism exactly — same structure, variable perceptual experience depending on where attention is directed.
explanations.A: While this offers choice to the audience, the underlying structure is fixed; the variable is which performer is watched, not the emergence of pattern from near-identical material. It does not capture the 'process' quality or the near-identity mechanism.
explanations.B: Explicit early statement of themes is the opposite of the minimalist mechanism, which involves the gradual, attention-dependent emergence of pattern from near-identical material.
explanations.C: Steadily increasing tempo creating a uniform sense of urgency is the inverse of the principle: here every viewer experiences the same effect, whereas the passage emphasizes variable perceptual experience depending on where attention is directed.
explanations.E: Intensive interpretive effort by trained readers describes the decoding of vertical complexity — the kind of listening the passage attributes to serialism, not to minimalism's horizontal, perceptual approach.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A standard historical narrative is introduced, the two aspects of that narrative are each examined and found wanting, a more accurate account is proposed, and a limitation of even the more accurate account is identified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A standard historical narrative is introduced and accepted, the career of one composer is traced in detail, and the implications for contemporary music are assessed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critical controversy about a musical movement is introduced, several scholars' positions are summarized, and the author proposes a resolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A musical movement is introduced, its historical narrative is questioned on two counts, its genuinely original contribution is identified and illustrated, and a further oversimplification — this time by the movement's defenders — is noted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A musical movement is compared with a preceding movement, their respective merits are weighed, and a synthesis emphasizing their shared concerns is advanced.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the 'clean break' narrative. Paragraph 2 questions it on two counts: serialism was not monolithic, and audience alienation preceded serialism. Paragraph 3 identifies minimalism's genuine originality (perceptual agency) and illustrates it with Reich. Paragraph 4 notes that even the movement's champions reproduce an oversimplification. D tracks all four moves in order.
explanations.A: Close but imprecise: the passage's movement in paragraph 4 is not about a limitation of the 'more accurate account' proposed in paragraph 3; it is about a separate oversimplification committed by the movement's defenders. A conflates these two different critical observations.
explanations.B: The standard narrative is questioned, not accepted; and no single composer's career is traced in detail — Reich is used briefly as an illustration.
explanations.C: No named scholars' positions are summarized; the passage argues conceptually rather than by summarizing a scholarly debate.
explanations.E: The passage does not weigh the merits of serialism and minimalism as equals, and no synthesis is advanced; the structure is argumentative rather than comparative.
